subject: PSHE
title: Peer pressure and safe choices
theme_status: Original lesson grouping, not a verbatim scheme theme
credit: Lesson resource · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0: free for classroom use, share and adapt with credit, no resale
definition: Peer pressure is feeling pushed by people of a similar age to do or choose something. It can be direct, felt without a spoken demand, or happen online. A person can choose differently and ask for help. Other people's harmful behaviour is not their fault.
assertiveness: Being assertive means making a clear, respectful choice or request. It can use words, a note or a usual aid. It does not require a loud voice, eye contact or a confident feeling. A clear no should be respected. A person can seek help without saying no first.
types: Someone tells or keeps asking a person to choose something.
A person feels they must copy a group to fit in, even without a direct demand.
Pressure happens in an online message or post. It may also be direct or indirect.

cases.title: A repeated choice request
cases.text: An invented learner wants the quiet drawing task. Another learner keeps asking them to choose a group task instead. The learner wants to keep their own choice.
cases.clue: Repeated requests try to change the learner's choice.
cases.response: No, I am choosing my own task.
cases.next: If asking continues or the learner wants support, they can tell trusted school staff privately.

cases.title: A group makes the same choice
cases.text: An invented learner sees a group choose the card tower task. No one tells them to join. They feel they must choose it to fit in, but they would like drawing.
cases.clue: The learner feels they must copy the group, without a spoken demand.
cases.response: No, I am choosing my own task.
cases.next: The learner can choose drawing or ask a trusted adult to help. Choosing the same task freely is also fine. The group is not automatically doing something wrong.

cases.title: A request about private work
cases.text: In an invented online chat, a learner gets repeated requests to share unfinished work they want to keep private. No actual message, account or work is shown.
cases.clue: Repeated online requests push the learner to share private work.
cases.response: Please stop asking. I want to keep my work private.
cases.next: Stop replying and ask a trusted adult for help with safe report or block tools. Do not send the content on.

phrases: No, I am choosing my own task.
Please stop asking. I want to keep my work private.
I am going to ask a trusted adult for help.
practice: Offer all three assertive phrases aloud in this calm lesson, using only the invented scenes. Staff give a neutral cue such as Try phrase one. No pupil acts as a person applying pressure. A learner can read, use a usual aid, type, point to a phrase, listen to a staff model, observe or pass. No one has to speak publicly, raise their voice, repeat a refusal or confront anyone. Record actual mode and prompts honestly. Practice is not proof of real-world safety or confidence.
success: Spot a pressure clue in all three invented cases, noting that types can overlap.
Choose a clear, respectful phrase and take part in each phrase opportunity in a valid mode.
Explain when and who to tell, using a safe route without needing to confront anyone.
help: Tell a trusted adult or school staff privately if pressure continues, feels confusing, makes someone uncomfortable or involves an unwanted online request. Help is valid even when unsure and before a refusal. Use words, a note, HELP or the usual aid. The safeguarding lead helps staff act through the school procedure. If the first adult is busy or help is not enough, ask another trusted adult. For an immediate safety concern, get adult help at once. Do not wait to repeat a phrase. An adult may need to share information with people who can help; no secret or fixed outcome is promised.
exit_card: The exit-line card is optional, private and pupil kept. Use a role, never a name. It may use the invented learner, stay blank or be passed. No personal pressure, account, worry or experience is needed. Do not collect, photograph, display, compare or copy it into learning evidence. An agreed scribe returns it to the pupil. A blank card is supported without pressing.
exit_route: The line I am going to ask a trusted adult for help is a reminder to use the agreed adult-supported route. Staff acknowledge the usual signal, keep supervision and support the familiar place or private conversation. A pupil does not leave alone. No one must say a line to the person applying pressure or remain in an unsafe situation.
step_out: Before teaching, agree a discreet HELP or PAUSE signal, available adult and familiar supervised place and route. Staff acknowledge it quietly. No public reason is needed. Offer a neutral task, supported return or private catch-up. Do not send a learner away alone. Pass and a pause are not failure.
safeguarding: Any disclosure goes to the safeguarding lead through school procedure. Listen calmly, reassure, do not probe, investigate or promise secrecy. Follow urgent school procedures for immediate concerns. Keep real concerns and identifying details in the separate safeguarding record, not learning evidence. A pupil unable to identify a trusted adult is supported privately, not pressed.

routes.Supported: Choose map B or advice C. Keep the short bank, starter and visible model. Offer two type or phrase choices if needed. Point, type, use a usual aid or exact scribe and readback. Offer all three phrase trials without pressure. Record content cues apart from usual access.
routes.Independent: Choose either format for all three cases. Explain type, clue, fitting phrase and safe next step. Offer all three phrase trials. Keep normal aids and the model. No personal story or public speech is needed.
routes.Aspire: Choose either format for all three cases. Explain why online pressure can be direct or indirect, and why a group sharing a choice is not always applying pressure. Adapt the help route if the first adult is busy. Offer all three phrase trials with usual access. No extra personal detail.

scaffolds.model: They can choose drawing and ask for help.
Repeated requests are a direct pressure clue.
No, I am choosing my own task.
They feel they must copy to fit in.
For case C, stop replying and ask staff for help.
Please stop asking. I want to keep my work private.
They can ask another trusted adult if help is not enough.

hinge.question: A group chooses the same task. One learner feels they must copy it to fit in. What is the best explanation?
choices: A The group must be doing something wrong.
B The learner may feel indirect pressure. They can choose differently or ask for help.
C The learner must copy the group.
D The learner must argue until everyone changes.
hinge.parallel: Repeated online requests push a learner to share private work. A This can be online and direct pressure. Ask a trusted adult for help. B Online pressure cannot be direct.
hinge.rule: Check privately. B or safe equivalent with a reason: proceed. A labels the group without evidence; C removes choice; D asks for control or conflict. Re-model and use parallel A. Pass or no response is unobserved and revisited with support, not failure.

timing: Settle, agree private help and supervised pause; recall free choice.
Teach direct, indirect and online pressure; types can overlap.
Model case A and a clear phrase. Match a clue or improve advice.
Check indirect pressure and free choice; choose task and mode.
22–27 map or advice for A to C; 27–32 offer all three phrases aloud with access alternatives; 32–34 optional private exit card.
Use common checks; set one NS and retain the pupil response.
Explain a help route or repair a pressure myth. Close with support.
where_this_leads: This helps me state a choice, respect another person's choice and seek support in a group or future work.
marking: Retain actual fictional learning evidence, usual access and content prompts. Record each phrase opportunity as spoken, aided, typed, pointed, model heard, observed, passed or not observed. A pass is not failure. Set one NS and allow a reply in the pupil's own colour or usual mode. E only for actual saved work. R only after Voice, Audience, one NS and the actual pupil response. Offer to the Communication portfolio; staff confirm mapping. Private cards and real concerns are not learning evidence.

paragraphs: Peer pressure is feeling pushed by people of a similar age to do or choose something. It can be direct, felt without a spoken demand, or happen online. A person can choose differently and ask for help. Other people's harmful behaviour is not their fault. Being assertive means making a clear, respectful choice or request. It can use words, a note or a usual aid. It does not require a loud voice, eye contact or a confident feeling. A clear no should be respected. A person can seek help without saying no first.
Someone tells or keeps asking a person to choose something.
A person feels they must copy a group to fit in, even without a direct demand.
Pressure happens in an online message or post. It may also be direct or indirect.

Online describes where pressure occurs. It can also be direct or indirect. In B, feeling a need to copy is a clue to indirect pressure, but the group is not automatically acting wrongly. A free choice to join a group is valid.

Direct pressure. Repeated requests try to change the learner's choice. Possible phrase: No, I am choosing my own task. If asking continues or the learner wants support, they can tell trusted school staff privately.
B A group makes the same choice

Indirect pressure. The learner feels they must copy the group, without a spoken demand. Possible phrase: No, I am choosing my own task. The learner can choose drawing or ask a trusted adult to help. Choosing the same task freely is also fine. The group is not automatically doing something wrong.
C A request about private work

Online pressure, also direct. Repeated online requests push the learner to share private work. Possible phrase: Please stop asking. I want to keep my work private. Stop replying and ask a trusted adult for help with safe report or block tools. Do not send the content on.

For all three invented cases, show the pressure type, a clue, a fitting phrase and a safe next step. Types can overlap. Both main formats have the same checks. All three phrase trials are offered in the learner usual mode. Accept other safe phrases and explanations. A map needs no art skill; advice needs no extra length. Each format covers A, B and C and all phrase opportunities.

Main B. A labels the group without evidence. C removes free choice. D asks the learner to control others. Re-model, then use parallel A: online and direct may overlap. A pass is unobserved. Check privately with usual access.

Assertiveness is not a volume, eye-contact or confidence test. A refusal should be respected. No one has to say no first or repeat it before asking for adult help. Never blame someone if pressure or harm continues.
No, I am choosing my own task.
Please stop asking. I want to keep my work private.
I am going to ask a trusted adult for help.

Offer all three assertive phrases aloud in this calm lesson, using only the invented scenes. Staff give a neutral cue such as Try phrase one. No pupil acts as a person applying pressure. A learner can read, use a usual aid, type, point to a phrase, listen to a staff model, observe or pass. No one has to speak publicly, raise their voice, repeat a refusal or confront anyone. Record actual mode and prompts honestly. Practice is not proof of real-world safety or confidence.

Use supplied mild cases only. Read cards with books, a usual aid or exact scribe if display or typing is unavailable. Staff give neutral phrase cues. Do not ask learners to persuade each other, raise voices, touch, open accounts or use a real event. A response may be private, aided, typed, observed or passed. Ask an adult at once if unsafe; no confrontation or repeated refusal is required.

The exit-line card is optional, private and pupil kept. Use a role, never a name. It may use the invented learner, stay blank or be passed. No personal pressure, account, worry or experience is needed. Do not collect, photograph, display, compare or copy it into learning evidence. An agreed scribe returns it to the pupil. A blank card is supported without pressing. The line I am going to ask a trusted adult for help is a reminder to use the agreed adult-supported route. Staff acknowledge the usual signal, keep supervision and support the familiar place or private conversation. A pupil does not leave alone. No one must say a line to the person applying pressure or remain in an unsafe situation.

Tell a trusted adult or school staff privately if pressure continues, feels confusing, makes someone uncomfortable or involves an unwanted online request. Help is valid even when unsure and before a refusal. Use words, a note, HELP or the usual aid. The safeguarding lead helps staff act through the school procedure. If the first adult is busy or help is not enough, ask another trusted adult. For an immediate safety concern, get adult help at once. Do not wait to repeat a phrase. An adult may need to share information with people who can help; no secret or fixed outcome is promised.

All cases are made up. No real account, message, work or personal story is shown. Use only these cases for class tasks.
An invented learner wants the quiet drawing task. Another learner keeps asking them to choose a group task instead. The learner wants to keep their own choice.
B A group makes the same choice
An invented learner sees a group choose the card tower task. No one tells them to join. They feel they must choose it to fit in, but they would like drawing.
C A request about private work
In an invented online chat, a learner gets repeated requests to share unfinished work they want to keep private. No actual message, account or work is shown.

Being assertive means making a clear, respectful choice or request. It can use words, a note or a usual aid. It does not require a loud voice, eye contact or a confident feeling. A clear no should be respected. A person can seek help without saying no first.

A group chooses the same task. One learner feels they must copy it to fit in. What is the best explanation? A The group must be doing something wrong. B The learner may feel indirect pressure. They can choose differently or ask for help. C The learner must copy the group. D The learner must argue until everyone changes. Check privately. B or safe equivalent with a reason: proceed. A labels the group without evidence; C removes choice; D asks for control or conflict. Re-model and use parallel A. Pass or no response is unobserved and revisited with support, not failure.

Repeated online requests push a learner to share private work. A This can be online and direct pressure. Ask a trusted adult for help. B Online pressure cannot be direct. Correct A. Online and direct can overlap. A pass is unobserved.

F Who could the invented learner tell? M What is the clue in B? H Why can C be online and direct, while a group making one choice is not always applying pressure? Use a note, pointing, typing or usual aid. No public questioning.

Being assertive does not require a loud voice, eye contact or a confident feeling. A person can get help without saying no first. Online pressure may also be direct or indirect. A group sharing a choice is not always applying pressure.

Cognition and Learning: short parts, visible model and two choices. Communication and Interaction: wait time, usual aid, typing or exact scribe with private readback. EAL: explain the key words and plan in any language.
